Pipeline stage: cut scores and decision quality

Source: R/pipeline-cuts.R
set_cuts.Rd

Records the cut scores that turn scores into decisions (pass/fail or performance levels) and estimates how accurate and consistent those decisions are. Cut scores come from a standard-setting study such as Bookmark or Angoff (item_map() gives the ordered item booklet for a Bookmark panel); give them directly, or give the panelists' ratings in panel and the cuts are their means.

Usage

set_cuts(
  p,
  cuts = NULL,
  scale = c("theta", "raw"),
  labels = NULL,
  panel = NULL,
  form = NULL,
  theta = NULL
)

Arguments

p

a calibrated pipeline from calibrate().

cuts

the cut scores, in increasing order. Can be omitted when panel is given.

scale

"theta" (ability, on the bank scale if linked) or "raw" (summed score on the test or form, where a score at or above the cut is in the higher category).

labels

names of the categories, one more than the number of cuts. Defaults to "Level 1", "Level 2", and so on.

panel

optional ratings from a standard-setting panel: a matrix or data frame with one row per panelist and one column per cut, on the same scale as cuts.

form

optional number of a fixed form from assemble_forms(); the decision quality is then estimated for that form instead of the calibrated test.

theta

optional population of abilities to average over (for example draws from the expected test-taker distribution).

Value

The pipeline with p$cuts: a list with the cuts on both scales (table), overall decision quality (summary), results by cut (by_cut) and the share of the population expected in each category (categories).

Details

Decision quality is estimated from the IRT model over a population of abilities (by default the calibration sample's EAP estimates, on the bank scale if the pipeline is linked):

  • With cuts on the ability scale (scale = "theta"), Rudner's (2001) method: the ability estimate is taken as normal around the true ability with the standard error from the test information.

  • With cuts on the summed-score scale (scale = "raw"), Lee's (2010) method: the summed-score distribution at each ability comes from the Lord-Wingersky recursion, and the true category is set by the expected (true) score.

Classification accuracy is the probability that the observed decision matches the true one; classification consistency is the probability that two parallel administrations give the same decision. Both are reported overall and for each cut, with Cohen's kappa for consistency and the false positive and false negative rates at each cut.

The checks (thresholds from mv_rules()):

  • class_accuracy (review): overall accuracy below cut_accuracy.

  • class_consistency (review): overall consistency below cut_consistency.

  • cut_precision (review): the standard error of measurement at a cut is above cut_sem; the test has too little information there.

  • panel_agreement (info): the panelists' cuts have a standard deviation (in ability units) above panel_sd.

References

Lee, W.-C. (2010). Classification consistency and accuracy for complex assessments using item response theory. Journal of Educational Measurement, 47(1), 1-17.

Rudner, L. M. (2001). Computing the expected proportions of misclassified examinees. Practical Assessment, Research, and Evaluation, 7, Article 14.

Examples

# \donttest{
p <- add_responses(mv_pipeline(), certexam, items = 3:34, key = certexam_key)
p <- calibrate(drop_items(p, "Q14"), model = "2PL")
p <- set_cuts(p, cuts = 20, scale = "raw", labels = c("Fail", "Pass"))
#> Warning: Cut scores is running with 1 review open flag(s) from earlier stages:
#>   #2 [review] local_dependence: Q21 & Q22 (Q3 = 0.27)
#> Flags only warn because strict = FALSE. See flags(p).
p$cuts$summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   accuracy consistency kappa
#>      <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1    0.881       0.836 0.620
p$cuts$by_cut
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>     cut label accuracy consistency kappa false_positive false_negative
#>   <int> <chr>    <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>          <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1     1 Pass     0.881       0.836 0.620         0.0863         0.0331
# }
